transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-10-05 15:30 UTC
Duration: 1h07m
Location: Zoom (recording available)
Shared artifacts: scheduler-knobs.pdf, atlas-token-dist.csv, example-traces.zip

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on throughput at high concurrency. Primary themes: tuning max_num_seqs to avoid GPU OOM and head-of-line blocking; reducing cold-start latency via pre-warm and KV cache priming; continuous batching trade-offs for tail latency; small notes on quantization enabling memory headroom; VPC/on-prem pinch points for warmstart and image pull time.

Topics covered (rough):
- Current production pain: spikes causing long tails and occasional OOMs when many short requests hit at once
- Scheduler knobs: max_num_seqs, token limits, per-queue concurrency, priority preemption
- Cold-start mitigation: warm pools, preloading KV cache for common prefixes, checkpoint prefetching
- Quantization and memory headroom: 4-bit vs 8-bit trade offs for batch sizing
- Observability: traces, p99, token histograms, scheduler metrics to track

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: All right, thanks everyone for joining. we'll run about an hour — real quick intros?
[00:12] Tom Hsu: Tom, Atlas CTO, Hey. we run the recommendation engine and shop assistant, lots of short prompts, like 20-80 tokens most of the time.
[00:22] Priya Nair: Priya, platform eng, we manage the inference infra and the k8s cluster that fronts the calls.
[00:28] Jon Mellor: Jon, SRE, we own on-call for the service.
[00:32] Miguel Santos: Miguel from Redwood SE, hi all, I'll drive the tuning details and sim results.
[00:38] Aisha Verma: Aisha here, solutions eng.
[00:41] Lena Park: Cool. so from your pre-read you said the p99 spikes with traffic bursts? can you give a real example?

[00:47] Tom Hsu: Yes, we saw a run yesterday where a marketing campaign — a spike of many concurrent small requests — p50 stayed fine but p95/99 ballooned to 1.8s, and once we hit say 1.2M tokens/minute the GPU would sometimes OOM. we use open models, quantized to int8, and a custom prefix cache layer.

[01:08] Miguel Santos: Couple of immediate suspects: 1) max_num_seqs configured too high so GPU memory usage for KV grows with concurrent sequences; 2) cold-starts when new workers come up and KV cache is empty; 3) continuous batching heuristics that overpack sequences and cause big seq-length variance inside batch.

[01:27] Priya Nair: we currently run max_num_seqs at 256 because we wanted high throughput but maybe that's too permissive.

[01:34] Miguel Santos: 256 can be fine for long sequences on A100s but if many tiny requests come in, the gpu's per-seq KV overhead multiplies. max_num_seqs is essentially a cap on concurrently tracked KV sequences; higher = more parallelism but more memory.

[01:50] Jon Mellor: is that distinct from batch_size? We think batching is handled continuously.

[01:55] Miguel Santos: yes, batch_size is number of tokens in a jit’d kernel call; continuous batching groups requests into windows. max_num_seqs limits how many open seqs can be aggregated across time. If you allow too many sequences, KV cache and attention state blow up.

[02:15] Lena Park: For your workload — lots of short requests — sometimes smaller max_num_seqs with faster dispatch reduces p99. it’s a counterintuitive tradeoff: you give up a bit of throughput for much better tail latency.

[02:30] Tom Hsu: hmm, we care about both. our SLO is 500ms p99. if lowering max_num_seqs reduces throughput too much we'll lose TPS.

[02:38] Miguel Santos: Right, so we usually pair a lower max_num_seqs with more aggressive batching window tuning and prefix caching. Important knobs: max_num_seqs, token_limit_per_request, continuous_batching_window_ms, and per-worker preemption threshold.

[02:56] Aisha Verma: Can you walk through a concrete config suggestion?

[03:00] Miguel Santos: Sure. Given your token distribution (thanks for the CSV), median ~45 tokens, 95th 120 tokens. Start with max_num_seqs=64, continuous_batching_window_ms=15, token_limit_per_request=1024, and enable prefix/KV priming for top-200 frequent prompts. Run a load test with those and check p99.

[03:22] Priya Nair: Why 64?

[03:25] Miguel Santos: 64 keeps KV state bounded and makes memory usage predictable — on an A10 it usually leaves headroom to handle bursts without preempting other workloads. If you need more parallelism we can scale nodes horizontally (more GPUs) rather than raising max_num_seqs.

[03:40] Tom Hsu: Is there a simulator or trace tool to estimate expected p99 before we change prod?

[03:45] Miguel Santos: Yes, we have an internal simulator that replays token-level traces and models KV growth. I'll run it against your csv and share histograms. It also simulates cold-cache scenarios — important to catch cold-start tails.

[04:00] Jon Mellor: Cold-start — what's our best mitigation? we saw nodes taking up to 4-6s to start handling traffic when scaled up.

[04:08] Miguel Santos: Cold-start length depends on two things: container/VM startup and runtime model/KV initialization. For VPC/on-prem the image pull can dominate if you don't keep a warm pool. For containerized Dedicated we recommend warm pool of idle workers that keep the model loaded and a small pre-warmed KV cache for most common prefixes.

[04:28] Lena Park: two practical items: maintain a minimum warm workers per region (keep some GPUs occupied at low load), and prime the KV cache: send low-cost priming requests during quiet times to populate frequent prefixes.

[04:40] Priya Nair: How do we prime KV without using a lot of tokens/cost?

[04:44] Miguel Santos: Use short priming requests that contain only the prefix you expect. The runtime charges tokens, but priming can be batched and rate-limited. Another approach is to snapshot the KV state for the top prefixes and load it at startup — that's a feature in Private deployments (load precomputed KV).

[05:03] Tom Hsu: ooh, snapshot KV load at startup — is that supported in Hosted?

[05:08] Miguel Santos: Hosted doesn't currently allow arbitrary KV snapshots for security/isolation reasons, but Private/Dedicated can. For Hosted we do warm pools and priming. For Private you can store and preload checkpointed KV state — much faster warmstart.

[05:22] Priya Nair: Any tips on setting continuous batching window? 15ms seems low, we were at 50ms.

[05:27] Miguel Santos: The window trades off throughput and latency. With many small requests a shorter window reduces head-of-line wait and reduces batch seq-length variance, which helps p99. But it can reduce throughput. For Atlas, try 15-25ms to start. The runtime also supports adaptive windowing: it shrinks the window when backlog is low and expands under heavy load. We can enable that heuristics flag for you.

[05:50] Aisha Verma: We use int8 quantization. does 4-bit help here?

[05:54] Miguel Santos: 4-bit can buy memory headroom, letting you increase max_num_seqs safely. But it can introduce small quality regressions for some prompts. For short queries it usually works fine. We recommend running a small A/B with typical prompts. Another hybrid is per-layer mixed precision quantization: critical layers stay 8-bit.

[06:16] Tom Hsu: If we move to more GPUs vs increasing max_num_seqs, what's the cost vector look like?

[06:21] Lena Park: we'll send a back-of-envelope cost estimate. horizontal scaling increases fixed infra cost but gives more isolation — less risk of single-node OOM. Increasing max_num_seqs is cheap but risks unpredictable memory blowups. We'll include both options in the estimate.

[06:36] Jon Mellor: Observability — what metrics should we watch to detect imminent OOM?

[06:41] Miguel Santos: Key ones: per-GPU KV memory used, number of open sequences per worker, continuous_batching_queue_depth, per-seq avg KV footprint, and request-level token histograms. Also set alerts on worker OOM events and rapid increases in open sequences.

[06:57] Priya Nair: Any suggestion for token caps to avoid runaway requests?

[07:00] Miguel Santos: token_limit_per_request is your friend. start with 1024 and monitor rejection rates. Also set soft caps with stream truncation and hard caps to protect the runtime. For recommendation UIs short caps are fine.

[07:12] Tom Hsu: We talked about per-queue preemption. how disruptive is preemption to a client?

[07:18] Miguel Santos: Preemption can drop or fall back requests depending on policy. Best practice: fall back to a smaller model or route to a different priority queue rather than drop. We can set a graceful degradation: if worker is overloaded, immediate short requests get priority, long gen gets shifted to lower priority queue.

[07:34] Miguel Santos: Also note that max_num_seqs interacts with KV eviction policy. If eviction is too aggressive you lose cache hit-rate, which increases token compute. If it's too lax you risk memory saturation.

[07:46] Aisha Verma: Are there production examples for cold-cache mitigation?

[07:50] Miguel Santos: One customer precomputes KV for top 1k intents and stores them; on startup they restore these into warm workers — p99 improved from 900ms to 140ms for small request mix. It's an operational lift but powerful.

[08:05] Tom Hsu: For the sim — can you model both warm and cold cache events?

[08:09] Miguel Santos: yes, the sim can replay traces with a configured cold-start rate (e.g., 5% of requests hit a cold worker). We'll run both no-warm and warm-pool scenarios so you can see the delta.

[08:20] Priya Nair: VPC/on-prem specifics — we have an air-gapped cluster in APAC where image pull takes long. Any suggestions?

[08:27] Miguel Santos: For air-gapped infra we recommend keeping a local image registry and maintaining a small persistent warm pool so you don't pay image pull time. Also consider preloading model shards to NVMe so load is faster. On-prem package supports preseeded model caches.

[08:43] Tom Hsu: security question — if we snapshot KV state, is that considered sensitive? it may contain user prefixes.

[08:49] Miguel Santos: Good point. KV snapshots must be handled carefully. Private deployments can store snapshots encrypted with KMS and you can control access. We suggest sanitizing or hashing user-specific tokens in the prefix data. We can also do a sanitized prefix-only snapshot for common system prompts.

[09:06] Jon Mellor: Ok that helps. what about continuous batching heuristics — you mentioned adaptive windowing, any other heuristics?

[09:12] Miguel Santos: There are a few: adaptive window ms, max_tokens_per_batch cap, seq-length bucketing (pack similar-length sequences), and priority slotting (short requests get assigned to fast lanes). The runtime supports sequence bucketing which reduces padding overhead and reduces kernel strain.

[09:29] Aisha Verma: Sequence bucketing — does that increase latency for some requests?

[09:32] Miguel Santos: Slightly, because the runtime may wait a small extra ms to find similar-length sequences. But the reduced padding tends to net lower p99 for workloads with mixed lengths. It's a tradeoff worth testing.

[09:45] Tom Hsu: How do we measure kv cache hit-rate?

[09:49] Miguel Santos: Runtime emits kvcache_hits, kvcache_misses per worker and a prefix-hit histogram. You can tie that with request IDs to see impact on latency. I recommend instrumenting a dash that shows hit-rate vs p99 over time.

[10:03] Miguel Santos: Quick note about quantization: if you go to 4-bit, watch activation memory and do A/B on quality. On our quantized benchmarks for short prompts, 4-bit p95 quality delta was <1% on a typical completion metric but some edge prompts failed.

[10:20] Priya Nair: Let's talk fallback routes if a worker hits OOM mid-request.

[10:24] Miguel Santos: We implement failure policies: immediate fail, retry on different worker, or graceful fallback to a smaller model. We recommend retry to a fallback queue with a short time backoff to avoid thundering herd. Also keep per-request idempotency keys so retries are safe.

[10:38] Tom Hsu: Ok. can you summarize a pragmatic first-pass config for us to validate in staging?

[10:43] Miguel Santos: Sure — pragmatic baseline for Atlas staging: max_num_seqs=64, continuous_batching_window_ms=20, adaptive_window=true, token_limit_per_request=1024, enable seq-length bucketing, kvcache_enabled=true with top-200 priming, quantization int8 with option to A/B 4-bit on a canary pool, warm_pool_min=2 workers per region.

[11:05] Lena Park: We'll include that in a checklist. Miguel, you'll run the sim and return histograms?

[11:10] Miguel Santos: Yup, I'll run the sim on their trace and include both warm and cold scenarios plus a variant with max_num_seqs=128 so they can compare.

[11:18] Tom Hsu: And timeline? we'd like results by next week.

[11:21] Lena Park: We'll aim to get the sim and a cost estimate by 2025-10-09.

[11:27] Priya Nair: Any gotchas for Dedicated vs Hosted?

[11:30] Miguel Santos: Hosted offers warm pools but not KV snapshot restore; Dedicated/Private gives more control — you can preload KV, tune eviction aggressively, and run custom startup scripts to speed image load. However Dedicated requires more ops work to maintain warm pools.

[11:46] Aisha Verma: One more quick question — are there scheduler metrics that can be exported to Prometheus?

[11:50] Miguel Santos: Yes. runtime exposes metrics with prometheus names: redwood_scheduler_queue_depth, redwood_open_sequences, redwood_kv_memory_bytes, redwood_batch_window_ms, kvcache_hits_total, etc. We'll share the metrics map.

[12:02] Tom Hsu: Great. wanted to confirm we can do per-route packing? we have high-priority routes that need low latency.

[12:08] Miguel Santos: Yes per-route configs are supported: you can pin routes to dedicated queues with different max_num_seqs and priority slots. That’s the recommended approach for latency-sensitive endpoints.

[12:18] (cross-talk, brief)
[12:22] Jon Mellor: Real quick — how big are the KV entries per sequence? ballpark?

[12:26] Miguel Santos: Depends on model and seq-length. Ballpark per-seq KV can range from 40KB to 200KB. Short sequences on decoder-only models tend toward the lower end. That’s why many short sequences can multiply memory fast.

[12:40] Tom Hsu: ok that explains the OOM spikes we saw.

[12:44] Miguel Santos: I'll also recommend a guardrail: set an operator-level alert when redwood_open_sequences approaches 80% of expected max_num_seqs capacity.

[12:53] Priya Nair: Do you have a recommended stress test script?

[12:56] Miguel Santos: We'll send a step function load generator that replays tokens per request with configurable concurrency and cold-start rate. It can also simulate different seq-length mixes.

[13:06] Tom Hsu: Anything else on quantization and batching?

[13:09] Miguel Santos: If you pick 4-bit, increase validation on quality and watch the long-tail prompts. For batching, prioritize seq bucketing and adaptive windowing.

[13:18] Lena Park: Ok let's go to action recap — I'll read back the next steps.

[13:22] Lena Park: Redwood: run sim on Atlas token distribution with warm/cold variants and max_num_seqs=64/128; share histograms and recommended config by 2025-10-09. Share scheduler knob guide and prometheus metric names. Provide cost estimate for horizontal scaling vs increased max_num_seqs.

[13:37] Tom Hsu: Atlas: share full traffic trace and confirm pilot window; provide p99 SLO and any compliance constraints for Private trial.

[13:45] Miguel Santos: We'll also propose a staging config file and a small canary test plan — 10% traffic to a canary queue.

[13:53] Priya Nair: Sounds good. thanks everyone.

[13:57] Lena Park: Thanks all. we'll follow up in email with links and timeline.

[end of recording]
